blocks.content: Soil conservation is an essential strategy to prevent soil erosion and maintain ecological balance for sustainable agriculture.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Soil erosion involves the detachment and transportation of topsoil by running water, wind, and human activities.
Water erosion manifests primarily as sheet erosion over gentle slopes and gully erosion forming ravines in steep terrains.
The Chambal basin in central India represents one of the most severe examples of gully erosion and badland topography.
Mechanical and biological conservation methods include contour ploughing, terrace farming, strip cropping, and afforestation.
Shelterbelts and windbreaks are critical conservation techniques in arid regions like Western Rajasthan to prevent wind erosion.

rows: Uniform removal of a thin layer of topsoil over a broad area
Cutting of deep channels or ravines by concentrated running water
Hard to detect immediately; leads to insidious loss of soil fertility
Highly visible, forming deep trenches that fragment land
Gentle slopes with sparse vegetation cover
Steep slopes and loose, clayey soils (e.g., Chambal Basin)
Cover cropping, mulching, and organic manure application
Construction of check dams, gully plugging, and terracing

items: Sheet Erosion vs Gully Erosion: Sheet erosion removes topsoil uniformly without distinct channels, while gully erosion carves deep channels rendering land unfit for cultivation.
Contour Ploughing: Ploughing along contour lines decelerates water flow on hill slopes and is frequently asked in UPSC and State PSC exams.
Chambal Ravines: A prime example of Badland Topography resulting from extensive gully erosion.
Government Initiatives: Soil Health Card Scheme (2015) and PMKSY (Per Drop More Crop) are key schemes associated with soil health and conservation.
